title: The history of the mosquito coil
tagline: Two hundred years from a daisy ground into powder to a spiral that billions light at dusk, and the science still catching up with it.
intro: People in the Caucasus and Persia knew that a certain daisy, dried and powdered, killed lice and fleas. In the 1880s a Japanese farmer mixed the powder into incense so its smoke would reach mosquitoes, and his wife's idea of winding the stick into a spiral made it last the night. Chemists then learned to build the daisy's molecules, nerve scientists worked out how they act, and doctors started asking two harder questions: what does the smoke do to people, and does keeping mosquitoes off really prevent disease?

eras.name: Daisy powder
eras.summary: Pyrethrum daisies are grown, dried and ground into insect powder, first in the Caucasus and Dalmatia, then sold across Europe. Someone tries burning it.

eras.name: From stick to spiral
eras.summary: Pyrethrum reaches Japan. An incense stick that kills mosquitoes becomes a spiral that burns all night, in the same years that the mosquito is proved to carry malaria.

eras.name: Chemistry and nerves
eras.summary: The daisy's molecules are drawn, copied and improved. Machines stamp out coils, electric mats do without the ember, and scientists find the nerve gate that pyrethroids jam.

eras.name: Evidence and resistance
eras.summary: Treated bed nets transform malaria control. The smoke from coils is measured, mosquitoes evolve resistance, and reviewers ask what coils have actually been proved to do.

events.title: Insect powder becomes a trade
events.who: Growers and merchants of the Caucasus
events.text: Dried, ground flower heads of the red Persian pyrethrum daisy had long been used against lice and fleas in the Caucasus and Persia. Commercial growing is recorded in Armenia from about 1828, and the product reached Europe as "Persian powder".
events.why: A flower turned out to hold one of the safest insect-killers ever found.

events.title: The Dalmatian daisy takes over
events.text: Around 1840 a white daisy from the Adriatic coast, Tanacetum cinerariifolium, was brought into cultivation. Its flowers hold more of the active pyrethrins than the Persian kind, and it became the world's pyrethrum plant.
events.why: Every pyrethrum crop since, from Japan to Kenya, has been this species.

events.title: Zacherlin: powder from a factory
events.text: Johann Zacherl, who had traded pyrethrum powder from Tiflis since 1842, opened a factory in Vienna to make an insect powder he called Zacherlin. It sold across Europe.
events.why: Insect powder became a branded household product.

events.title: Burn it instead: the first fumigating cones
events.text: An Italian pharmacist pressed pyrethrum powder into small cones to be burnt in a room. The smoke carried the insecticide to flying mosquitoes that powder on a shelf could never reach.
events.why: The idea of delivering pyrethrum by smouldering it was born.

events.title: Seeds cross the Pacific
events.who: Eiichiro Ueyama and H. E. Amoore
events.text: Eiichiro Ueyama, a mandarin-orange grower, met the American seed trader H. E. Amoore in 1885 and agreed to swap seeds. In 1886 a packet arrived that included pyrethrum, and Ueyama harvested his first flowers the next year.
events.why: Japan would become the world's biggest pyrethrum grower within thirty years.

events.title: The first mosquito incense stick
events.text: Ueyama mixed pyrethrum powder into incense-stick paste and sold the result as a mosquito stick, which his company calls the world's first. It worked, but a thin stick burned out in well under an hour.
events.why: It joined two old crafts, incense and insect powder, into one product.

events.title: Yuki Ueyama suggests a spiral
events.text: A longer, thicker stick would last the night but would be fragile and awkward. Ueyama's wife, Yuki, proposed winding it into a spiral, and trials began. The company applied for a patent in 1900.
events.why: A spiral packs a night-long strip into the space of a saucer.

events.title: The mosquito is caught carrying malaria
events.text: Working in an army hospital in Secunderabad, Ronald Ross dissected a dappled-winged mosquito that had fed on a malaria patient and found the parasite in its stomach wall. The next year, in Calcutta, he showed mosquitoes passing malaria between birds. He won the Nobel Prize in 1902.
events.why: Once the mosquito was known to be the carrier, keeping it off people became a public health goal.

events.title: The spiral coil goes on sale
events.text: After years of trials the hand-wound spiral coil reached shops. Workers rolled the paste into long ropes and coiled two at a time, a method that lasted more than fifty years.
events.why: It is the same product, in the same shape, that billions of people still light.

events.title: The daisy's molecules are drawn
events.text: Two chemists, both later Nobel laureates, published the structures of pyrethrin I and II, the main insect-killing molecules of pyrethrum. Details were corrected by Frederick LaForge and W. F. Barthel in the United States in 1944.
events.why: Knowing the structure made it possible to try building copies.

events.title: Kenya starts exporting pyrethrum
events.text: Pyrethrum was planted in Kenya's cool highlands in the late 1920s and exports began in 1933. When war cut off Japanese supplies, Kenya became the world's main source; its harvest peaked at 15,300 tons in 1975.
events.why: The natural insecticide became an African cash crop.

events.title: Japan's record pyrethrum harvest
events.text: Japan had been the largest producer since about 1914. In 1938 it gathered a record 13,200 tons of dried flowers, and more than half went to the United States.
events.why: Natural supply was at its limit just as war was about to cut it off.

events.title: DDT's power is discovered
events.text: At the Geigy company, Paul Müller found that DDT, a compound first made in 1874, killed insects on contact and went on working for months. It won him the 1948 Nobel Prize and reshaped malaria control. It also acts on the sodium channels of insect nerves.
events.why: A cheap, lasting insecticide made spraying houses the main weapon against malaria.

events.title: Allethrin: the first man-made pyrethroid
events.text: Milton Schechter's group synthesised allethrin, a simplified copy of pyrethrin I. It was the first pyrethroid. Sumitomo Chemical began making it in Japan in 1953, and from about 1955 it started to replace daisy powder in coils.
events.why: Coils no longer depended on a harvest of flowers.

events.title: Flies that will not fall
events.text: James Busvine reported house flies that DDT and pyrethrins could no longer knock down. The trait, later named knock-down resistance or kdr, was traced by the 1950s to a single gene, and much later to the sodium channel itself.
events.why: It was the first warning that insects evolve their way out of nerve poisons.

events.title: India launches a national malaria programme
events.text: With an estimated 75 million cases a year at independence, India began a National Malaria Control Programme in 1953 and raised it to an eradication programme in 1958, built on spraying houses with DDT. Reported cases fell to under 50,000 in 1961, then surged back to about 6.5 million in 1976.
events.why: It showed both how much insecticides could do and how quickly gains could be lost.

events.title: Machines take over from hand-winding
events.text: Until the 1950s every coil was rolled and wound by hand. In 1957 Kincho completed an automatic machine that punched the interlocked double spiral out of a flat sheet.
events.why: The nested pair you snap apart today is the shape that punching made natural.

events.title: The electric mat: vapour without an ember
events.text: Fumakilla launched Vape, described as the world's first electric mosquito killer: a small pad soaked in pyrethroid, warmed on a hot plate. A first-generation Vape is kept in the Edo-Tokyo Museum.
events.why: The active could now be warmed into the air with no smoke from burning.

events.title: How it jams a nerve
events.text: Using the giant nerve fibres of squid and lobster, Toshio Narahashi and colleagues showed that allethrin and DDT keep a nerve's sodium current flowing after it should have stopped, so the nerve fires again and again.
events.why: It explained knock-down, and later why insects are about a thousand times more sensitive than mammals.

events.title: India's Insecticides Act
events.text: The Insecticides Act, passed in 1968 and brought into force in 1971, set up a Central Insecticides Board and a Registration Committee. Every insecticide product, household coils included, must be registered before it is made or sold.
events.why: It is why a legal coil carries an active ingredient, a strength and a registration number.

events.title: Pyrethroids that survive sunlight
events.text: Michael Elliott's group at Rothamsted Experimental Station published permethrin, "a photostable pyrethroid", in 1973, followed within a year by deltamethrin. Earlier pyrethroids broke down in hours outdoors; these lasted weeks.
events.why: They made pyrethroids the insecticides of farms, house walls and, later, bed nets.

events.title: A bed net dipped in insecticide
events.text: Researchers of the French institute ORSTOM working in Burkina Faso published the first village test of bed nets soaked in permethrin. Treated nets killed or drove off mosquitoes that plain nets only blocked.
events.why: It began the insecticide-treated net, now the main malaria tool worldwide.

events.title: An Indian Standard for coils
events.text: The Bureau of Indian Standards published IS 13438, a specification for allethrin mosquito coils, alongside one for mats. By then coils and electric mats were everyday goods in Indian cities; in 1994 Godrej bought Transelektra, the maker of a leading mat.
events.why: Coils became a standardised, regulated product in their biggest market.

events.title: Nets that stay treated for years
events.text: A WHO expert group reviewed the Olyset net, which has permethrin built into its fibres so that it survives years of washing. In 2007 the WHO advised that nets should be long-lasting, free or cheap, and used by everyone in a community.
events.why: It turned treated nets from a project into a mass programme.

events.title: The smoke is measured
events.who: Weili Liu, Junfeng Zhang and colleagues
events.where: New Jersey, United States, and Malaysia
events.text: A chamber study of six coil brands from China and Malaysia found that one coil gives off as much PM2.5 mass as 75 to 137 cigarettes, and as much formaldehyde as up to 51. A companion paper warned of coils abroad containing a synergist, S-2, that can form a potent lung carcinogen when it smoulders.
events.why: It put numbers on a trade-off users had only smelt.

events.title: Resistance gene found in India's malaria mosquito
events.who: Om P. Singh and colleagues, National Institute of Malaria Research
events.text: Researchers found the first direct evidence of a kdr mutation in Indian Anopheles culicifacies, the main rural malaria mosquito, in a population resistant to DDT and deltamethrin. In 2015 the same group reported kdr mutations in Delhi's dengue mosquito, Aedes aegypti.
events.why: Pyrethroids, in coils, sprays and nets alike, were losing some of their grip.

events.title: A coil that smokes far less
events.who: Lin Zhang, Junfeng Zhang and colleagues
events.text: Tests showed that a coil with a charcoal-powder base gave off 12.6 mg of fine particles an hour, against 63 to 127 mg for ordinary sawdust-base coils. The paper also passed on an industry estimate: 45 to 50 billion coils used each year by about 2 billion people.
events.why: The smoke is not fixed: it depends on what the base is made of.

events.title: 663 million cases averted
events.who: Samir Bhatt and colleagues, Malaria Atlas Project
events.text: A study in Nature estimated that malaria control prevented 663 million cases in sub-Saharan Africa between 2000 and 2015. Insecticide-treated nets accounted for 68% of them.
events.why: It is the strongest evidence that keeping mosquitoes off sleepers saves lives at scale.

events.title: India sets a date to end malaria
events.who: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
events.text: India launched its National Framework for Malaria Elimination 2016-2030. Reported cases, 11.7 lakh in 2015, fell below 2 lakh by 2020, then rose again to about 2.6 lakh in 2024.
events.why: The goal moved from control to elimination.

events.title: "We do not know"
events.who: Marta Maia and colleagues, Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group
events.text: A Cochrane review found only two trials of coils against malaria, in China and Indonesia, with results too uncertain to trust. It concluded: we do not know if coils protect against malaria. An earlier review had found consistent evidence that coils do reduce biting.
events.why: It drew the honest line between stopping bites and proving that disease is prevented.

events.title: WHO backs spatial emanators
events.text: After a trial in western Kenya in which a passive transfluthrin emanator cut new malaria infections in children by about a third, the WHO gave a conditional recommendation for spatial emanators used indoors together with nets, and approved the first two products.
events.why: The coil's principle, a faint repellent vapour in a room, got its first formal backing, in a smokeless form.

series.title: Malaria cases reported in India
series.caption: Cases reported to the national programme each year. They fell by more than nine-tenths between 1995 and 2021, then edged up. The true number of infections is higher than the number reported.

facts: The spiral was not the inventor's idea. Eiichiro Ueyama made mosquito sticks; his wife Yuki suggested coiling them.
A coil's glowing tip would destroy its insecticide. The active escapes as vapour from the warm strip a few millimetres ahead of the ember.
For more than fifty years every mosquito coil was rolled and wound by hand. Machines took over only in 1957.
Pyrethroids are copies of molecules made by a daisy to defend itself against insects.
By one industry estimate, people light 45 to 50 billion coils a year.
